meta.titre: Population and Labour: age structure, dependency and labour supply
meta.sous_theme: Population structure, dependency ratio and labour supply

sections.contenu_markdown: In a family compound in Bafoussam, some members go to school, some work in the market or in offices, and some are too old to work. The working members must feed and support the others, and the same pattern exists in the whole country. How many people work compared with how many depend on them helps a government decide how many schools, clinics and jobs to plan. GCE papers ask for definitions (youthful and aging population, immigration and emigration), for calculations of the dependent population from percentages, and for the factors that change the supply of labour.

items: To find a percentage of a number, multiply the number by the percentage and divide by 100.
A census is a count of all the people living in a country.
People need food, schooling and health care whether or not they earn an income.

sections.titre: Population structure, dependency and the supply of labour
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Population and its change
The population is the total number of people living in a country at a given time, counted in a census. It changes through births, deaths and migration. The birth rate and the death rate are the numbers of births and deaths per 1,000 people in a year. Natural increase is the birth rate minus the death rate. Immigration is the entry of people into a country to settle; emigration is the departure of people from a country to settle elsewhere. Net migration is immigrants minus emigrants.

### Age structure

| Group | Who | Economic role |
|---|---|---|
| Young | Too young to work | Dependants |
| Working age | Old enough and not yet retired | Producers who support the others |
| Aged | Retired | Dependants |

The exact age limits differ from country to country, so questions give the percentages. The **dependent population** is the young plus the aged. The **working population** (labour force) is the part of the population that is able and willing to work, whether employed or looking for work. The **dependency ratio** is the number of dependants for every 100 workers:

$$\text{Dependency ratio} = \frac{\text{dependent population}}{\text{working population}} \times 100$$

A *youthful* population has a large share of young people: schools are in great demand and future workers are many, but dependants are numerous. An *aging* population has a large share of old people, usually because birth rates are low and people live longer: pensions and health care cost more and there are fewer workers.

### Supply of labour
The quantity of labour depends on the size of the population, its age structure, the school-leaving age (a higher one delays entry into work), the retirement age (a higher one adds working years), the number of women who take jobs, and migration. The quality of labour depends on education, training and health. Higher wages in a job also attract more workers into that occupation.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the command word is distinguish, differentiate or give the difference between
variantes.contenu_markdown: Define both terms and join them with a contrast word such as "whereas" or "while". Each term needs its own definition; one sentence about only one term earns few marks.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the population and the percentages of three age groups are given
variantes.contenu_markdown: Check that the percentages total 100. Add the young and aged percentages, then take that percentage of the population. Subtract the result from the total to find the working population. For the dependency ratio, divide the dependants by the workers, not by the whole population.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question mentions overpopulation or underpopulation
variantes.contenu_markdown: The optimum population is the size that gives the highest output per head with the available resources and technology. A population above it is overpopulation (too many people for the resources, so output per head falls); a population below it is underpopulation (resources are not fully used).

sections.enonce_markdown:
A country has a population of 50 million. Of these, 38% are below working age, 55% are of working age and 7% are aged.
(a) Calculate the dependent population.
(b) Calculate the working population.
(c) Calculate the dependency ratio.
(d) State whether the population is youthful or aging.

etapes.justification: The three groups must make up the whole population.
Dependants are the young plus the aged.
Divide dependants by workers, then multiply by 100.
The largest dependent group is the young.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Young people are 38% against 7% aged, so the population is **youthful**.

sections.conclusion_markdown: (a) 22.5 million. (b) 27.5 million. (c) About 82 dependants for every 100 workers (81.8). (d) Youthful, because the young are by far the larger group of dependants.

items.erreur_markdown: "The dependent population is the number of young people."
items.pourquoi_faux: The aged also depend on others for support.
items.correction_markdown: Dependent population = young + aged. In the example above it is $38\% + 7\% = 45\%$ of the population.

items.erreur_markdown: "Emigration means people coming into a country."
items.pourquoi_faux: The two words are reversed. Emigration begins with the idea of exit.
items.correction_markdown: Emigration is leaving a country to settle elsewhere; immigration is entering a country to settle.

items.pourquoi_faux: The ratio compares dependants with workers, not with the whole population. Dividing by 50 gives the share of dependants, not the ratio.

items.erreur_markdown: "A youthful population is one in which people live to a great age."
items.pourquoi_faux: Living long describes an aging population. Youthful refers to a large proportion of young people.
items.correction_markdown: A youthful population has a high proportion of young people, usually because birth rates are high.

items.erreur_markdown: "Raising the school-leaving age immediately increases the number of people available for work."
items.pourquoi_faux: Young people stay in school longer, so they enter the labour force later.
items.correction_markdown: It reduces the quantity of labour in the short run, although it may improve the quality of labour later through education.

items.enonce_markdown: A country has a population of 40 million. Of these, 30% are young, 62% are of working age and 8% are aged. Calculate (a) the dependent population and (b) the working population.

A country has a population of 10 million at the start of the year. Its birth rate is 36 per 1,000 and its death rate is 14 per 1,000. During the year 30,000 people immigrate and 50,000 emigrate.
(a) Calculate the natural increase per 1,000 and in numbers.
(b) Calculate net migration.
(c) Calculate the population at the end of the year.

Country A has 30 million people: 40% young, 54% working age, 6% aged. Country B has 12 million people: 18% young, 60% working age, 22% aged.
(a) Calculate the dependency ratio of each country, to one decimal place.
(b) Say which country has a youthful population and which has an aging population.
(c) State one economic problem facing each country.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Country A: dependants $= 40 + 6 = 46\%$ of 30 million $= 13.8$ million; workers $= 54\%$ of 30 million $= 16.2$ million; ratio $= \frac{13.8}{16.2} \times 100 =$ **85.2**.
Country B: dependants $= 18 + 22 = 40\%$ of 12 million $= 4.8$ million; workers $= 60\%$ of 12 million $= 7.2$ million; ratio $= \frac{4.8}{7.2} \times 100 =$ **66.7**.
(b) A is **youthful** (40% young); B is **aging** (22% aged).
(c) Country A: heavy demand for schools, health care for children and jobs for new workers. Country B: high spending on pensions and health care for the old, with a smaller share of people to pay taxes.

items_markdown: Population changes through birth rate, death rate and migration. Natural increase is birth rate minus death rate; net migration is immigrants minus emigrants.
Immigration is entry to settle in a country; emigration is departure to settle elsewhere.
Dependent population is the young plus the aged; the dependency ratio divides dependants by workers and multiplies by 100.
A youthful population has many young people (high birth rates); an aging population has many old people (low birth rates and longer life).
Labour supply in quantity depends on population size, age structure, school-leaving and retirement ages; quality depends on education, training and health.
